idea.text: Acids and alkalis cancel each other out: they neutralise. In a titration you add alkali from a burette, a little at a time, to an exact volume of acid until it is just neutralised. An indicator changes colour at that moment, and the volume used tells you how strong the acid is.
idea.analogy: Like filling a glass to the brim in dim light: pour fast at first, then drop by drop near the top, because one drop too many and it overflows.

steps.title: Fill the burette
steps.instruction: Fill the burette with 0.100 M NaOH. Pour slowly through the funnel.

whatIf.rate: Pouring fast into the narrow burette funnel makes it overflow, splashing corrosive alkali, often near face height. Pour slowly, with the burette below eye level.

explore.if: fill the burette above eye level
explore.then: Any overflow runs down towards your face. Lower the burette, or stand so its top is below your eyes while you fill it.

explore.if: leave the funnel in the burette
explore.then: Drips from the funnel can fall into the burette during the titration and change the volume you read. Take it out after filling.

steps.title: Clear the air bubble
steps.instruction: Open the stopcock fully and run a little NaOH into the waste beaker to clear the air bubble from the tip.

whatIf.order: The burette needs to be filled before there's anything to run through it.

explore.if: leave the air bubble in the tip
explore.then: The bubble gets pushed out during the titration, so the scale says more liquid went in than really did. Your titre comes out too big.

steps.title: Read the burette
steps.instruction: Read the initial volume at eye level, to the nearest 0.05 mL.

whatIf.reading: Reading from above or below eye level shifts the number you see (parallax). Bend down so your eye is level with the bottom of the curved surface, the meniscus.
whatIf.order: Read the starting volume only after the bubble has been cleared, otherwise the bubble is counted in your reading.

explore.if: read the top of the meniscus instead of the bottom
explore.then: Every reading shifts by the same amount, so the difference (the titre) can still be right, but only if you read it the same way every time.

steps.title: Pipette 10.00 mL of acid
steps.instruction: Use the pipette filler to draw 10.00 mL of HCl, bottom of the meniscus on the mark.

whatIf.overshoot: The pipette is made to measure one exact volume. If the meniscus isn't on the mark, the amount of acid is wrong, and so is every calculation after it.
whatIf.quantity: The pipette is made to measure one exact volume. If the meniscus isn't on the mark, the amount of acid is wrong, and so is every calculation after it.

explore.if: use a measuring cylinder instead of a pipette
explore.then: A cylinder is only accurate to about ±0.5 mL, so your acid volume could be 5% out. A pipette is accurate to about ±0.05 mL.

steps.title: Deliver into the flask
steps.instruction: Let the pipette drain into the rough conical flask.

whatIf.order: Fill the pipette with acid before trying to empty it into the flask.
whatIf.quantity: If some acid is left behind or spilt, the flask has less than 10.00 mL and the titre comes out too small.

explore.if: blow out the last drop from the pipette
explore.then: Pipettes are made to leave that last drop in the tip. Blowing it out adds extra acid, so the titre comes out slightly too big.

whatIf.order: Put the acid in the flask first, then the indicator.
whatIf.overshoot: A few extra drops won't change much, but indicators are weak acids themselves, so a lot of indicator uses up a little extra alkali.

explore.then: Universal indicator changes gradually through many colours, so there's no sharp moment to stop. Phenolphthalein snaps from colourless to pink.

steps.title: Flask on the white tile
steps.instruction: Stand the flask on the white tile under the burette.

explore.then: The first faint pink is much harder to see against a dark bench, so you're more likely to go past the end point.

steps.title: Rough titration
steps.instruction: Add NaOH about 1 mL at a time, swirling, until the pink colour stays.

whatIf.order: Read the burette and get the acid and indicator ready before adding any alkali, or you won't know how much you used.
whatIf.portion-too-big: Big portions overshoot the end point by more, so the rough result is less useful. About 1 mL at a time, swirling in between.
whatIf.no-mixing: Without swirling, the alkali sits in one patch that turns pink while the rest of the flask is still acidic. You might stop too early.

explore.then: You wouldn't know where the end point is, so you'd have to add every drop slowly from the start. The rough run saves time and stops you overshooting.

steps.title: Read the rough titre
steps.instruction: Read the burette again. Rough titre = final - initial.

whatIf.reading: Reading from above or below eye level shifts the number you see (parallax). Bend down so your eye is level with the bottom of the curved surface, the meniscus.

steps.title: Pipette 10.00 mL again
steps.instruction: Rinse, then pipette another 10.00 mL of HCl.

whatIf.overshoot: If the meniscus isn't on the mark, the flask gets the wrong amount of acid and the accurate titre won't match the rough one.
whatIf.quantity: If the meniscus isn't on the mark, the flask gets the wrong amount of acid and the accurate titre won't match the rough one.

explore.then: Leftover water inside dilutes the acid you draw up, so there are fewer moles of acid and the titre comes out too small.

steps.title: Deliver into a clean flask
steps.instruction: Drain the pipette into the second conical flask.

whatIf.order: Fill the pipette with acid before trying to empty it into the flask.
whatIf.quantity: If some acid is left behind or spilt, the flask has less than 10.00 mL and the titre comes out too small.

whatIf.order: Put the acid in the flask first, then the indicator.

steps.title: Swap flasks on the tile
steps.instruction: Put the second flask on the white tile.

explore.then: The first faint pink is much harder to see against a dark bench, so you're more likely to go past the end point.

steps.title: Accurate titration
steps.instruction: Run in quickly to about 1 mL before the rough end point, then add dropwise, swirling after every drop, until a faint pink lasts 30 s.

whatIf.order: Finish the rough run and set up the second flask first: you need the rough titre to know when to slow down.
whatIf.not-dropwise: Near the end point a single drop changes the colour. A stream here sails past it, so the titre comes out too big and the acid seems stronger than it really is.
whatIf.overshoot: Once you're past the end point you can't go back: the flask is now alkaline. The titre is too big, so you'd calculate the acid as stronger than it is. Undo, or start a new flask.
whatIf.no-mixing: Unmixed drops make a pink patch that fades when you swirl. Swirl after every drop so you see the true colour of the whole flask.
whatIf.quantity: A titre that's off means the acid's concentration you calculate will be off by the same proportion.

explore.if: add the alkali faster near the end
explore.then: You'd overshoot. The extra alkali after the end point still counts in your reading, so the acid looks more concentrated than it is.

explore.if: stop at the first pink flash
explore.then: A pink flash that disappears when you swirl means acid is still left. Wait for a faint pink that lasts 30 seconds.
Each mL now carries twice as many OH⁻ ions, so you'd need about half the volume. The answer for the acid would come out the same.

steps.title: Final reading
steps.instruction: Read the burette. Titre = final - rough final reading.

whatIf.reading: Reading from above or below eye level shifts the number you see (parallax). Bend down so your eye is level with the bottom of the curved surface, the meniscus.

explore.if: take away the wrong starting reading
explore.then: The titre is the final reading minus the reading at the start of that run. Mixing them up gives a volume that means nothing.

fill-1.text: What could go wrong if you pour quickly into a narrow tube?

fill-2.text: Tilt the bottle only a little so the pour-rate gauge stays green, below 6 mL/s.

fill-3.text: Watch: a slow, steady pour into the funnel.

bubble-1.text: Look closely at the tip below the stopcock. Is it full of liquid?

bubble-2.text: Open the stopcock fully for a moment over the waste beaker. The rush of liquid pushes the air out.

bubble-3.text: Watch the stopcock open fully, then close.

read-1.text: Where should your eye be when you read a scale?

read-2.text: Open the lens, slide to eye level and read the bottom of the meniscus to the nearest 0.05 mL.

read-3.text: Watch the reading lens line up with the meniscus.

pipette-1.text: A pipette is accurate only to its line. How do you hit it exactly?

pipette-2.text: Draw above the mark with the filler, then let it fall until the bottom of the meniscus sits on the line.

pipette-3.text: Watch the meniscus settle on the mark.

ind-1.text: Indicators are strong dyes. How much do you need?

ind-2.text: Squeeze the dropper bottle for 2 or 3 drops only.

tile-1.text: How will you spot the first faint pink?

tile-2.text: Drag the flask onto the white tile under the burette tip. It snaps into place.

tile-3.text: Watch the flask snap onto the tile.

rough-1.text: This run only needs to find roughly where the end point is.

rough-2.text: Add about 1 mL, swirl, and repeat until the pink stops fading.

acc-1.text: What happens if you add too much at once near the end point?

acc-2.text: Slow down! Near the end point add one drop at a time with the stopcock, swirling after each drop.

acc-3.text: Watch the last millilitre go in drop by drop.

observations.whatHappened: Each drop of alkali flashed pink where it landed and faded when you swirled. At the end point a single drop turned the whole flask a faint pink that lasted.
observations.why: H⁺ ions from the acid and OH⁻ ions from the alkali combine to make water. While acid is left over, any pink is neutralised as soon as it mixes in. When the moles of NaOH added equal the moles of HCl in the flask, the next drop leaves the solution slightly alkaline and phenolphthalein turns pink above about pH 8.2.
realWorld: Checking acidity in fruit juice and wine

prompts.question: Why did a pink flash appear where each drop landed, then fade when you swirled?
choices: Locally there was excess alkali until it mixed with the acid
prompts.explain: Right where it lands, the drop of NaOH is in excess, so the indicator turns pink. Swirling mixes it into the acid, which neutralises it.

prompts.question: At the end point, the moles of NaOH added are...
choices: Equal to the moles of HCl
Equal to the volume of HCl
prompts.explain: HCl and NaOH react 1 : 1, so at equivalence the moles are equal.

prompts.question: Your titre was about 10.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH for 10.00 mL of HCl. The acid concentration is closest to...

captions.text: Fill the burette slowly with 0.100 M sodium hydroxide.
captions.why: A burette adds liquid in tiny, measured amounts and lets you read how much you used, to 0.05 mL.
captions.safety: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive. Fill the burette below eye level using a funnel, and pour slowly so it can't overflow.

captions.text: Run a little through to clear the air bubble from the tip.
captions.why: An air bubble in the tip would be counted as liquid when you read the scale, so your result would be wrong.

captions.text: Read the starting volume at eye level: 1.00 mL.
captions.why: Read the bottom of the curved surface (the meniscus) with your eye level with it. Looking from above or below shifts the reading.

captions.text: Pipette exactly 10.00 mL of the acid into a conical flask and add phenolphthalein.
captions.why: A pipette measures one exact volume very accurately. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and turns pink once there is the slightest excess of alkali.
captions.safety: Always use a pipette filler, never your mouth.

captions.text: Rough run: about 1 mL at a time, swirling, until the pink stays.
captions.why: The rough run finds roughly where the end point is, so the accurate run can go quickly up to just before it.

captions.text: Accurate run: run in quickly to 9 mL...
captions.why: Up to about 1 mL before the rough end point there is still plenty of acid left, so nothing can go wrong yet.

captions.text: ...then drop by drop, swirling after each one.
captions.why: Near the end point a single drop (0.05 mL) is enough to tip the flask from acid to alkali. Swirling mixes each drop in before the next.

captions.text: A faint pink that lasts 30 seconds: the end point.
captions.why: Now the moles of NaOH added equal the moles of HCl in the flask. From the volume used you can work out the acid's concentration.
